screens.body:
Shipping code by hand — dragging files over FTP, SSH-ing into a server and hoping — is slow, scary, and easy to mess up.

CI/CD replaces hope with a pipeline: every change is built, tested, and shipped automatically. Same steps, every time, no 2 AM heroics.
screens.heading: The deployment problem

screens.body:
Continuous integration means: every time you push code, a server builds it and runs the tests automatically. Within minutes you know if you broke something.

The rule is simple: never let broken code sit. CI catches it while the change is still fresh in your mind.
screens.heading: CI: continuous integration
screens.keyPoint: Every push gets built and tested in minutes.

screens.body:
Continuous delivery means every tested change is ready to ship — often with one click. Continuous deployment goes further: tested changes ship automatically, no click needed.

Small, frequent releases beat giant scary ones. If something breaks, you know exactly which small change did it.
screens.heading: CD: delivery & deployment
screens.keyPoint: Small frequent releases beat giant scary ones.

screens.body:
A pipeline is a chain of stages, each gating the next: build → test → deploy to staging → deploy to production. If any stage fails, the chain stops.

That gating is the magic: broken code literally cannot reach users, because a failed test stage blocks the deploy stage.

code.snippet:
# a tiny pipeline: each stage gates the next
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

screens.heading: Anatomy of a pipeline
screens.keyPoint: Failed stage = stopped pipeline = users stay safe.

screens.body:
How you roll out matters. Big bang: everyone gets the new version at once (exciting, terrifying). Rolling: update servers a few at a time. Blue-green: run old (blue) and new (green) side by side, then flip traffic over.

Blue-green is the calmest: if green misbehaves, flip back to blue in seconds.

options: Runs old and new side by side, then flips traffic
Updates one user at a time
check.question: Blue-green deployment…

screens.heading: Deployment strategies
screens.keyPoint: Blue-green: run both, flip the switch.

screens.body:
Every deploy needs a rollback plan: if the new version breaks in production, how fast can you return to the last good version?

Teams practice rollbacks like fire drills. The question isn't if you'll need one — it's whether you'll be ready when you do.

options: Returns to the last good version fast
check.question: A rollback…

screens.heading: Always have a way back
screens.keyPoint: Plan the way back before you ship.

screens.body:
Your Learn SD Vercel deploy failed on "npm run build" — the build broke, and you only found out at deploy time. A CI pipeline would have run that same build on every push and told you in minutes.

When SwiftGigs launches, CI/CD means you can ship fixes to real users the same day — safely, with tests guarding the door.

options: On push, before deploy — in minutes
check.question: CI would have caught your Vercel build failure…

screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: CI catches broken builds before deploy time.
